findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the handler returns
findings.body: In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) the background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. As soon as the handler returns (which happens immediately, because the goroutine is fire-and-forget), net/http cancels the request context, and every context derived from it is cancelled too. The legacy store call will therefore frequently fail with `context canceled` (or never reach the DB at all), silently losing the legacy write that mode 3 exists to keep as a safety copy. The derived context must be detached from the request, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout (while still carrying the request's auth/user values).

findings.title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Object names are unbounded (one per resource instance), so each successful delete creates a new Prometheus label value, causing unbounded metric cardinality growth in the dual-writer histogram and skewing/polluting all dashboards built on the `kind` label. It should pass `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Create error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure happened in unified storage, not legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong store and no storage-error sample is recorded at all. Any alert/dashboard on storage error rate will miss these failures while the legacy error rate shows phantom errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: Update error path records a legacy-store duration for a storage failure
findings.body: On a failed `d.Storage.Update` the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The failing call was against unified storage, so storage errors are never recorded and legacy error metrics are inflated with failures that did not occur in legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration
findings.body: Inside the background goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore invisible, and the storage histogram is polluted with timings of legacy calls, making mode-3 metrics unusable for detecting broken legacy writes.

findings.title: Delete puts the wrong logger in the context
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the bare writer logger instead of the `log` built one line above with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that pulls the logger out of the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses all request-specific fields, making delete failures much harder to correlate. Every other method in this file passes `log`.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no lifecycle tracking
findings.body: The four write paths spawn bare goroutines calling into the legacy store. (1) A panic inside a legacy store implementation (e.g. nil map/pointer in the SQL layer) is not recoverable from the goroutine and will take down the whole Grafana process, whereas in the previous synchronous code the apiserver's handler recovery would have converted it to a 500. (2) Nothing tracks in-flight goroutines, so `Destroy()` (line 172) can tear down `d.Legacy`/`d.Storage` while a goroutine is still calling into them, and in-flight legacy writes are silently dropped on shutdown. A `defer recover()` plus a WaitGroup/semaphore drained in `Destroy()` is needed.

findings.title: Create passes the caller's object to the legacy store from a goroutine without deep-copying
findings.body: `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs concurrently with the request handler while `obj` is the very object the apiserver handler chain passed in; registry stores and legacy stores mutate the passed object (name from generateName, UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp). Sharing the pointer with a goroutine while the handler may still read/serialize or further mutate it is a data race (and makes the legacy row depend on timing). The object should be `obj.DeepCopyObject()`ed before handing it to the goroutine.

findings.title: Legacy update now reuses the raw objInfo instead of the object written to unified storage
findings.body: The previous implementation fetched the current object from storage and wrapped `objInfo` in an `updateWrapper` carrying the object actually persisted, so the legacy store received the same final state. The new code calls `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` with the original `objInfo`, which re-runs `UpdatedObject` against the legacy store's own old object. Consequences: for PATCH/apply requests the patch is re-applied to a possibly different base, and for requests that carry a resourceVersion the value refers to the unified-storage revision, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict. Either way legacy silently diverges from unified storage (the error is only counted in a metric, not even logged). Also note `objInfo` is a request-scoped object being invoked concurrently from the goroutine, which is not guaranteed to be safe for reuse.

findings.title: No test verifies that the asynchronous legacy write happens
findings.body: All mode-3 tests only assert the value returned from the unified-storage mock. Because the legacy write now happens in a detached goroutine, nothing in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests waits for or asserts `Legacy.*` was invoked (and `legacyStoreMock`/`storageMock` share one `mock.Mock`, so a legacy call cannot even be distinguished from a storage call). The whole point of mode 3 — that writes eventually reach legacy — is untested, so defects such as the cancelled-context issue in the goroutines cannot be caught by this suite. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage plus a channel/`assert.Eventually` to assert the legacy call.

findings.title: "unified store fails" test case only configures the legacy mock
findings.body: The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets up the failure via `setupLegacyFn` and leaves `setupStorageFn` nil; it only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the legacy expectation also satisfies the storage call. The test therefore does not actually exercise a unified-storage failure and would keep passing if the storage error path regressed. The same pattern appears in the List test case whose name still says "is not implemented" even though List is now implemented.

findings.title: go.work.sum changes look accidental and add a duplicate entry
findings.body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` even though the identical line already exists immediately above, and adds hashes for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, older otel versions) that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. These lines are probably the result of a local `go work sync` with a different module set; they are out of sorted order and the duplicate will be removed again by tooling. Revert the go.work.sum changes unless a dependency actually changed in this PR.
